terms.definition: A write changes data; a read returns it. Replication treats the two differently.
The point at which a transaction's changes become permanent on a database.
Promoting another copy to take over when the main database fails.

before.note: Read Databases first: replication keeps the transaction and durability promises you learned there across more than one machine. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: A single database is a single point of failure: if its machine dies, the data is unreachable and maybe lost. PostgreSQL's documentation opens by describing two goals for servers that work together: allowing a second server to take over quickly if the primary fails, which is high availability, and allowing several computers to serve the same data, which is load balancing [[pg-solutions]]. Replication keeps extra copies on other machines, kept up to date with the first.

The usual shape is one primary that accepts writes and one or more replicas that copy those writes and serve reads. PostgreSQL calls servers that can modify data read/write, master or primary servers, and servers that track changes in the primary standby or secondary servers [[pg-solutions]]. MySQL uses the terms source and replicas, and says replication is asynchronous by default [[mysql-repl]].

Replication buys two things: durability and availability, by having copies survive a machine loss, and read scaling. MySQL lists scale-out among its advantages, with all writes and updates taking place on the source and reads spread across replicas [[mysql-repl]]. It does not by itself let you store more data than one machine holds; that is sharding, a later topic. Replication is about copies of the same data, not splitting it.

terms.definition: The database copy that accepts writes and is the source of truth. Also called the leader or master.
A copy that follows the primary's changes and can serve reads. Also called a follower or standby.
The stream of changes the primary ships to replicas so they can apply the same writes.
Spreading read queries across replicas to handle more read traffic.
Keeping the service up through failures by having a copy ready to take over.

reading.what: The goals of high availability and load balancing, and the terms primary and standby.
The source and replica shape, that replication is asynchronous by default, and the advantages MySQL lists.

canNow: Say why one database is a single point of failure.
Explain what replication gives you and what it does not.

stages.name: How it works
body: The primary records every change in an ordered log and streams it to the replicas, which replay the same changes in the same order. PostgreSQL's standbys read the primary's write-ahead log, which the page describes in terms of continuous archiving and streaming replication [[pg-warm-standby]]. MySQL says its traditional method replicates events from the source's binary log [[mysql-repl]]. Either way the replica rebuilds the primary's state by applying the log.

Replication can be asynchronous or synchronous. Asynchronous means the primary commits and tells the client done without waiting for replicas, which is fast but means a replica can lag behind; MySQL says replication is asynchronous by default [[mysql-repl]]. PostgreSQL describes the synchronous option: each commit of a write transaction waits until confirmation is received that the commit has been written to the write-ahead log on disk of both the primary and the standby, and data can then be lost only if both are damaged at once [[pg-warm-standby]]. That protects against losing the commit on failover but makes every write wait.

The gap between a replica and the primary is replication lag. PostgreSQL's page describes it as the amount of WAL records generated on the primary but not yet applied on the standby, which you can calculate by comparing the primary's current WAL write location with the last location received by the standby [[pg-warm-standby]]. Under asynchronous replication a read sent to a lagging replica can return data slightly out of date, so a user who just wrote something might not see it on the next read.

When the primary fails, a replica is promoted to be the new primary, a failover. PostgreSQL's page says a standby leaves standby mode and switches to normal operation when pg_ctl promote is run or pg_promote() is called [[pg-warm-standby]]. If replication was asynchronous, any writes the old primary had not yet shipped are lost. Setups weigh how much they are willing to lose against how much they are willing to slow every write to avoid it.

terms.definition: The primary commits without waiting for replicas; fast, but replicas can lag and a crash can lose recent writes.
The primary waits for a replica to confirm before committing; safer on failover, slower per write.
How far behind the primary a replica is, measured in time or in log position.
Making a replica the new primary, usually during failover.
The ordered record of changes the primary ships to replicas to replay.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Reading from replicas introduces a subtle correctness issue: read-your-writes. If you write to the primary and then read from a lagging replica, you may not see your own change. Common fixes are routing a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, or waiting for the replica to catch up to the write's log position before reading. These are general techniques, not something the cited pages describe.

A single-primary design avoids write conflicts, since only one machine accepts writes, but makes the primary a bottleneck and a failure point until a replica is promoted. PostgreSQL's page describes the alternative: in asynchronous multimaster replication each server works independently and periodically communicates with the others to identify conflicting transactions, which can be resolved by users or by conflict resolution rules [[pg-solutions]].

Deciding who becomes the new primary safely is itself hard. If two nodes both think they are primary, they can accept conflicting writes, a split brain. Avoiding this needs agreement among the nodes, which is what consensus algorithms provide. The Raft project page describes consensus as multiple servers agreeing on values, where a decision, once reached, is final, and where typical algorithms make progress when any majority of servers is available [[raft-site]].

terms.definition: The guarantee that after you write, your own later reads see that write.
One node takes writes (no conflicts, one bottleneck) versus several (more capacity, write conflicts to resolve).
Two nodes each believing they are primary and accepting conflicting writes.
Nodes agreeing on one value or one leader despite failures; Raft is one algorithm for it.
A majority of nodes that must agree, so two conflicting majorities cannot both form.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The governing trade-off is the one from the Databases topic made concrete: strong versus eventual consistency. Synchronous replication makes each commit wait for the standby's confirmation, which gives a current view and little loss but slows writes; PostgreSQL notes it also depends on the standby being reachable to confirm [[pg-warm-standby]]. Asynchronous replication keeps writes fast but lets replicas serve slightly stale reads. Which you choose depends on whether a stale read or a slow write hurts your application more.

Replication is also how backups and low-disruption maintenance work. MySQL says that because a replica can pause the replication process, you can run backup services on the replica without corrupting the source's data [[mysql-repl]]. A standby can be taken offline without stopping writes on the primary, and failover turns a dead primary into a short disruption rather than an outage, provided the promotion is handled cleanly and clients reconnect.

The hard limit to remember: replication multiplies copies of the same data but never shrinks the data set a single machine must hold. MySQL's own scale-out description keeps all writes on the source [[mysql-repl]]. When one machine can no longer hold or write all the data, you must split it, which is Sharding. Replication and sharding are usually combined, each shard being itself replicated.

terms.definition: How sure you are a committed write survives; stronger with synchronous replication, weaker with asynchronous.
A replica kept ready to be promoted, also usable for backups and maintenance.
Upgrading or repairing one copy while others keep serving.
A single shard of a split data set that is itself kept on several replicas.

misconceptions.myth: A replica is always an exact, up-to-the-moment copy.
misconceptions.truth: MySQL says replication is asynchronous by default, so replicas lag; PostgreSQL describes lag as WAL records generated on the primary but not yet applied on the standby [[mysql-repl]] [[pg-warm-standby]].

misconceptions.myth: Replication lets you store more data than one machine holds.
misconceptions.truth: Replication copies the same data to more servers. MySQL's scale-out model keeps all writes on the source, so storing more than one machine holds needs sharding [[mysql-repl]].

PostgreSQL says that with synchronous replication data can be lost only if both primary and standby are damaged at once; with asynchronous replication, writes the old primary had not yet shipped can be lost [[pg-warm-standby]].

misconceptions.myth: Any replica can safely decide to become primary.
misconceptions.truth: Without agreement two nodes can both claim to be primary. The Raft page describes consensus as servers agreeing on values, with a decision that is final once reached [[raft-site]].

tryIt.intro: These inspect replication on a running PostgreSQL primary and replica with psql. The PostgreSQL pages name the view pg_stat_replication and the functions below, and the statements are the usual ways to call them. Output depends on your setup, so it is not shown here.

commands.shows: On the primary, one row for each WAL sender process, which the page says you can list through this view.
On the primary, the current write-ahead log write location. The page compares it with the standby's last received location to see lag.
On a standby, the last write-ahead log location received and synced to disk by streaming replication.
Whether this server is still in recovery, which is true on a standby.
On a standby, the time stamp of the last transaction replayed, taken from when the commit was generated on the primary.
